title: The Good King
author: Matt Perrone
summary: Reflects on the archetype of Father Christmas and masculine leadership in family contexts. Uses J.R.R. Tolkien's tradition of writing Father Christmas letters to his children as a model—creative, personal, and present rather than transactional. Critiques modern consumer Christmas culture, which outsources magic to purchases, and contrasts it with the archetype of the Good King from 'Good King Wenceslas': a leader who sees the overlooked, steps into the cold, and presides over meaningful shared experience. Argues that fathers and family leaders are called to play this role not through perfect execution but through deliberate, creative presence. The crown of holly is not for the faint of heart; it asks men to build tradition, lead households, and create the conditions where family members encounter belonging and meaning.
points: Modern Christmas relies on consumer nostalgia and purchased magic rather than creative parental presence and deliberate tradition-making within families.
Tolkien's Father Christmas letters model an alternative: a father at his desk, writing imaginative tales for his children, making Christmas present and particular rather than generic and nostalgic.
The archetype of the Good King—wise, generous, willing to step into hardship for others—applies to contemporary fatherhood and family leadership, not as performance but as deliberate choice.
Father-leaders are asked to build traditions, preside over households, see the overlooked members, and create shared meaning—tasks that require creativity and presence, not just provision.
The gap between consumer Christmas and relational Christmas is a gap in masculine leadership: between outsourcing joy and building it, between passing through tradition and making it.
quotes: What a privilege! In most Christmas Carol adaptations, the ghost of Christmas Present looks like the 19th century conception of Santa Claus/Father Christmas: a man both wise and jolly, with a crown of holly.
The crown of holly is not for the feint of heart.
Our modern role of 'Father Online Shopping' has no saintly mantle at all.
Watching Home Alone with the ghost of Christmas Past for the 35th time is fine, fun even. But there are bigger games to play, taller tales to tell, richer songs to sing.
When Tolkien wrote his Father Christmas letters, he was not an accomplished author, he was just another dad.

It's not enough for us to base our Christmas tradition on nostalgia, and things we can only experience vicariously. Father Christmases of today are the Good, Benevolent, Creative, Jolly, Wise and Generous Kings.” Archived from Build the Village Substack on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
